The must-sees

  • Basilica of Saint-Sernin

    Church

    It was built for pilgrims on the road to Santiago de Compostela and holds the relics of Saint Saturnin. It is one of the largest Romanesque churches in Europe.

    Look for: On the south side, the Porte Miégeville has some of the earliest large Romanesque carving in France, with Christ rising between angels.

  • Canal du Midi

    Waterfront · 1681

    Pierre-Paul Riquet built it to link Toulouse to the Mediterranean, and it opened in 1681. It is listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.

    Look for: At the Port de l’Embouchure, three canals meet; a carved marble relief from 1775 celebrates the joining of the waterways.

  • Capitole

    Civic building

    It is named after the capitouls, the consuls who governed medieval Toulouse. The building also holds the Théâtre du Capitole and the Salle des Illustres.

    Look for: The eight pink marble columns on the facade stand for the eight capitouls who once ran the city.

  • Cité de l’espace

    Museum · 1997

    It opened in 1997 in a city at the heart of Europe’s space industry. Visitors can walk through a copy of the Mir space station.

  • Couvent des Jacobins

    Church

    It was the mother house of the Dominican order, founded in Toulouse. The relics of Thomas Aquinas have rested here since 1369.

    Look for: Step into the cloister, where brick arcades rest on slender paired marble columns.

  • Musée des Augustins

    Museum

    It became a museum during the Revolution, one of the first in France. Its Romanesque sculptures came from churches and cloisters across the city.

    Look for: In the cloister, a line of stone gargoyles taken down from old buildings stands along the gallery.

  • Place du Capitole

    Square

    The bronze cross in the centre was designed by the artist Raymond Moretti. Markets, concerts and crowds have filled the square for centuries.

    Look for: Walk under the arcades on the side facing the Capitole and look up: painted ceiling panels by Moretti tell the city’s history.

  • Pont Neuf

    Bridge

    It was begun in the 16th century and took nearly a century to finish. The openings let floodwater of the Garonne pass through.

    Look for: At the left-bank end, the round brick tower is a 19th-century water tower, now a photography gallery.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Toulouse and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Toulouse passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
